sentences.text: Akainacephalus johnsoni stands as the most complete ankylosaur skeleton ever recovered from southern Laramidia, preserving a full skull, tail club, and limb bones.
Its scientific name merges Greek terms for spine and head, a reference to the creature's spiky defensive covering.
The dinosaur featured enormous bony bosses above the eyes that merged into a high ridge stretching over the eye socket.
Unlike many relatives, the nostrils were small, tear-shaped holes completely hidden from the front view.
The defensive tail club was built from a handle of eleven fused vertebrae capped by a knob of three bony plates.
Rings of armor along the neck consisted of six fused plates that lacked the saw-tooth edges seen in some other species.
This specimen is renowned for its exceptional completeness, including parts of the pelvis and a full tail club.
The face displayed a unique armor pattern with pyramid-shaped scales on the forehead and a central row of cone-shaped scales on the nose.
Paleontologists Jelle P. Wiersma and Randall B. Irmis formally named and described this genus in 2018.
The nearly whole skeleton was dug up between 2008 and 2010 at the Horse Mountain Gryposaur Quarry within the Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument.
The very first ankylosaur bones at this specific site were found in 2008 by Scott Richardson, a worker for the Bureau of Land Management.
This armored dinosaur shared its environment with many other creatures, including the duck-billed Gryposaurus and the horned Utahceratops.
It also lived alongside giant crocodyliforms like Deinosuchus and various turtle species.
It is a single-species genus belonging to the ankylosaurid family, with Akainacephalus johnsoni being the only known member.
Taxonomists place this animal in the subfamily Ankylosaurini.
Earlier studies grouped it with Nodocephalosaurus in a southern Laramidian clade, positioning it as a base-line relative to Asian forms like Saichania.
Later research by Frauenfelder and colleagues suggested a different relationship, identifying it as a sister group to two other distinct lineages.
This creature inhabited southern Utah during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the late Campanian stage around 76.26 million years ago.
Its fossils come from the middle unit of the Kaiparowits Formation, an area that once held a humid coastal plain with rivers, lakes, and wetlands.
The climate was wet and humid, supporting a wide variety of life forms.
Scientists discuss whether ankylosaurines moved from Asia to North America once or at least twice, with some arguing for two separate migration events.
Park and colleagues proposed that these migrations happened before the Cenomanian stage, suggesting an early dispersal from Asia to western North America.
